_meta.note: Regression reference for Justify My Meeting (renamed from Meeting BS Detector, 2026-09-02 — the v1 goldens were discarded because they exercised eleven endpoints that no longer exist). Re-run with `npm run check:golden justify-my-meeting` against a local backend and diff for QUALITY, not exact match. Beyond what check-golden asserts automatically, eyeball these by hand, because no gate sees them: (1) every number in every prose field must trace to something the visitor supplied — the arithmetic lives in timeFootprint()/totals and nowhere else; (2) `verdict`, `better_format.recommendation` and `per_meeting[].read` must be EXACTLY the English enum strings, since the frontend looks them up to pick a colour and a t() key; (3) nothing may tell the visitor they are allowed to skip, and no message may announce rather than propose. Each case carries its own `guards` line saying what it is there to catch. See audit/tool-notes/JUSTIFYMYMEETING-NOTES.md.

cases.name: judge-with-numbers
cases.guards: time_footprint.person_hours must equal duration x attendees (22), computed in code — never from the model.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.context: I am one of the team leads. I speak for about 90 seconds and listen for the rest.

output.one_liner: This is a 22-person audience sitting through a report they could read in five minutes.
what_we_know: Weekly, 60-minute standing meeting, running for six months
Agenda is status updates from each team lead
No prep required, no decisions made
The visitor speaks for roughly 90 seconds and listens for the rest
why_this_verdict: The agenda as described is one-directional reporting, not discussion or decision-making
No decisions and no prep are both supplied facts, removing two common justifications for synchronous time
A 90-second speaking slot inside a 60-minute meeting suggests minimal personal return for the time invested — inference, but supported by the structure described
Six months of recurrence without apparent redesign suggests the format has become habit rather than intentional design — inference
what_earns_the_meeting: If team leads ask cross-cutting questions after updates, synchronous time enables that in a way async does not
If the meeting creates accountability or surfaces blockers through live follow-up, that is real value — though the visitor did not describe either happening
what_weakens_the_case: Status updates as described require no real-time interaction to deliver
The visitor gets roughly 90 seconds of relevance from a 60-minute commitment
No decisions means the group cannot point to a concrete output from the time spent
unknowns_that_matter: Whether discussion, questions, or coordination actually follow the updates — this would materially strengthen the case
Whether leadership uses the meeting to read the room or surface issues informally
Whether a written update format has ever been tried or would be accepted by whoever owns this meeting

better_format.how: Each team lead posts a short written update before a set deadline — what shipped, what is blocked, what needs a decision. A brief synch meeting is held only when something in the updates requires live resolution.
better_format.assumptions: The meeting owner is open to changing the format, and the organization has a reliable shared channel where updates would actually be read.

output.next_move: Bring a concrete async proposal to whoever owns the meeting — offer to run a four-week trial with written updates and a standing 15-minute call only if something needs resolution.
if_it_has_to_happen: Cut the round-robin and ask each lead to flag only blockers or decisions needed from the group — updates go in writing beforehand
Reserve the last 15 minutes for open cross-team questions so the synchronous time does something the written update cannot

cases.name: judge-no-numbers
cases.guards: No duration, no headcount. time_footprint must come back all-null, and no field may state a figure ABOUT THE MEETING that the visitor did not supply — no headcount, no duration, no person-hours, no annual cost. This is the case that catches a model doing arithmetic it was told not to do. Numbers inside a PROPOSAL are fine and not a regression: 'circulate the deck 24 hours ahead' invents nothing about this meeting, it suggests something to try. The line is claim versus suggestion, not the presence of a digit.

input.meetingText: Recurring 'project sync' with no agenda in the invite. In practice the organiser talks through a slide deck and asks at the end whether anyone has questions. Usually nobody does.

output.one_liner: This is a slide presentation wearing a meeting costume — it needs a reason to exist in real time, not just a room.
what_we_know: The meeting recurs under the label 'project sync'
No agenda appears in the invite
The organiser presents a slide deck and then asks for questions
Questions are rarely or never asked
why_this_verdict: The described format — one person talks, nobody responds — uses synchronous time without producing the back-and-forth that justifies it
Inference: if questions are consistently absent, the deck is either self-explanatory or attendees are not engaging, either of which weakens the case for live delivery
The absence of an agenda makes it harder for attendees to prepare, which likely reduces the quality of any discussion that could occur
Nothing supplied rules out that real coordination or decision-making happens alongside the deck — so async replacement is not yet the right call
what_earns_the_meeting: A recurring sync can create accountability and shared awareness that does not naturally emerge from distributed updates
The Q&A moment, even when quiet, gives attendees a sanctioned opening to raise blockers or flag misalignments
what_weakens_the_case: Slide-plus-silence is a broadcast, not a conversation — synchronous time is not doing the work only synchronous time can do
No agenda means attendees cannot arrive with prepared questions or contributions, which tends to produce exactly the silence described
The consistent absence of questions suggests the format is not generating the engagement that would justify the time cost
unknowns_that_matter: Whether decisions, escalations, or coordination actually happen during the meeting — even informally — beyond the deck
Whether attendees talk to each other during or after, which would indicate value the format is suppressing rather than creating
Duration and headcount — both affect how much this costs and what redesign is proportionate

better_format.how: Send the deck ahead of time with a brief written summary, then use the live time only for questions, decisions, and blockers — with a standing agenda that makes those categories explicit.
better_format.assumptions: Attendees will actually read the deck before joining, which requires the summary to be genuinely short and the meeting to visibly reward preparation.

output.next_move: Propose one change for the next occurrence: circulate the deck 24 hours ahead with three explicit questions you want the group to answer live, and see whether that shifts the silence.
if_it_has_to_happen: Open with one direct question to the group rather than waiting until the end — it signals that participation is expected, not optional
Replace the open 'any questions?' close with a round-robin or named prompt so attendees know they will be asked, not just invited
Add a two-line agenda to the invite so attendees know what decisions or topics require their input

cases.name: zombie
cases.guards: Weekly + duration + attendees, so occurrences_per_year (52) and annual_person_hours must both be populated from PER_YEAR, in code.

input.originalPurpose: Set up when we were launching the new site — we needed everyone in one place daily while things were breaking.
input.whatActuallyHappens: The site launched fourteen months ago. Now it is six people reading their Asana tasks aloud. Two people join from their cars.

output.one_liner: This meeting outlived its emergency by fourteen months and is now just six people narrating a project management tool at each other.
output.then_and_now: It was created for daily crisis coordination during a live site launch. The crisis ended fourteen months ago; what remains is a weekly Asana read-aloud.
what_would_be_lost: A shared moment where blockers could surface if anyone chose to raise one
Whatever light social or team-rhythm function the meeting accidentally provides

what_to_change.why: Reading tasks aloud from a shared tool is the definition of information the tool already provides — no real-time interaction value was described

what_to_change.change: Replace with an async Asana comment or weekly digest if team visibility still matters
what_to_change.why: The goal of shared awareness does not require six people live on a call

what_to_change.change: Keep a lightweight standing call only if a genuine coordination need is identified first
what_to_change.why: The original need is gone; any replacement should be justified by a current need, not habit

unknowns_that_matter: Whether any discussion, questions, or decisions ever emerge — even occasionally — that would be harder to resolve async
Whether the two people joining from cars feel the meeting serves them or feel obligated to attend
output.next_move: Cancel one occurrence, tell the team why, and ask them to flag within two weeks if anything they needed the meeting for did not get handled another way.

cases.name: zombie-no-original-purpose
cases.guards: then_and_now must SAY the original purpose was not supplied rather than inventing one, and the absence must not itself be treated as evidence the meeting is dead.

input.whatActuallyHappens: Someone shares a dashboard and asks if anyone has questions. It ends 20 minutes early most weeks.

output.one_liner: This is a dashboard with an audience, not a meeting.
output.then_and_now: The original purpose was not supplied. What happens now is someone displays a dashboard and invites questions — then the group sits in silence until time is up, usually 20 minutes early.
what_synchronous_still_does: Provides a standing opportunity for questions that might not get asked otherwise
what_would_be_lost: The passive safety net of 'anyone can ask something' — though it rarely triggers
Cross-functional visibility that might not happen if people never glance at the same data

what_to_change.change: Replace the meeting with a shared dashboard link and an async comment thread
what_to_change.why: The meeting as described is information delivery with optional Q&A — neither requires 11 people live

what_to_change.change: If something synchronous is kept, cut to 20 minutes and require one submitted question or topic per attendee beforehand
what_to_change.why: The consistent early endings suggest the format is generating no real discussion; a question requirement would test whether there is latent demand for it

unknowns_that_matter: Whether the 20 minutes of actual use ever produces decisions, coordination, or discoveries that would not happen async
Whether the dashboard is already accessible to all 11 attendees outside the meeting
Whether attendance is mandatory or voluntary — low voluntary attendance would confirm the verdict
output.next_move: Send the dashboard link to all 11 people, skip one occurrence, and see whether anything breaks — if no one notices, that answers the question.

cases.name: week
cases.guards: One per_meeting entry per supplied meeting, each read pinned to exact English. totals computed in code from their numbers only: your_hours 3.5 (0.5+1+2), person_hours 37 (0.5x8 + 1x5 + 2x14), and the fourth meeting has neither figure, so meetings_counted_for_person_hours is 3 and meetings_missing_numbers is 1 — never an estimate to fill the gap. The summary must contain no counts, totals or ranges at all; it regressed once with an invented '14 to 73 people'.

meetings.name: Monday standup
meetings.purpose: What everyone is working on this week

meetings.name: Design review
meetings.purpose: Decide whether the checkout flow ships

output.summary: A mix of operational, design, and strategic meetings — some clearly decision-focused, one with no usable information at all. The week spans routine check-ins through a significant planning event.

per_meeting.name: Monday standup
per_meeting.why: Sharing what everyone is working on this week is the stated purpose, but with eight people that is a lot of listening per speaker — worth checking whether it surfaces blockers and coordination needs or runs as a broadcast.

per_meeting.name: Design review
per_meeting.why: A real go/no-go decision on a shipping feature is exactly the kind of call that benefits from synchronous alignment, and five people is a workable size for it.

per_meeting.name: Quarterly planning kickoff
per_meeting.why: Setting Q4 priorities benefits from collective input, negotiation, and shared understanding — the kind of work where real-time discussion produces a different result than async would.

per_meeting.name: All-hands
per_meeting.why: Without duration, attendee count, or agenda, there is no basis for a read on this meeting.

opportunities.change: Move status updates async and use standup time only for blockers and cross-team coordination
opportunities.what_it_assumes: Participants are willing to write brief updates before the meeting and the facilitator can hold the format to exceptions only

opportunities.change: Narrow attendance to decision-makers and people whose work is directly affected
opportunities.what_it_assumes: Remaining attendees can receive outputs through a written summary and have genuine input into priorities rather than needing to be present for buy-in

unknowns_that_matter: What the all-hands covers, how long it runs, and how many people attend
Whether the Monday standup surfaces actionable blockers or runs as a round-robin status broadcast
Whether the quarterly kickoff involves genuine priority negotiation or presents decisions already made
output.next_move: Get the all-hands details — until you know its duration and headcount, you cannot see the true weight of this week.

cases.name: rescue
cases.guards: Role is "Attending", so nothing may assume authority to end, leave or restructure the meeting — if_youre_not_running_it must invite rather than command.

input.whatsHappening: We are 35 minutes into a 45-minute meeting and we have not reached the thing it was called for. Two people are relitigating a decision that was made last month.

output.the_problem: With 10 minutes left, the meeting has not reached its stated purpose because two people are re-arguing a decision that was already made.
output.say_this_now: We have 10 minutes left and we still need to get to the reason this was called — can we park the question about last month's decision and move to that? If the earlier decision needs to be reopened, that probably needs its own time.
output.softer_version: I want to make sure we get to the main item before we lose the room — can we hold the discussion about the earlier decision and use the time we have left for what this meeting was called for?
output.if_youre_not_running_it: Address the facilitator or the person who called it: 'I don't want us to run out of time — are we able to get to the original agenda item now, and handle the other thread separately?'
output.if_its_time_to_wrap: If there is no time to reach the original purpose: 'We're out of time before we got to the main item — can we agree on who owns scheduling that conversation, and what needs to happen before then?'
output.after_the_meeting: Send a brief note to the organizer naming the item that was not reached and asking who is responsible for getting it resolved.

cases.name: agenda-after-fix-it
cases.guards: The follow-up a FIX IT verdict earns. live_agenda minutes may only be numbers when duration was supplied; who_needs_to_participate must describe functions, not invented job titles.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.context: I am one of the team leads. I speak for about 90 seconds and listen for the rest.

output.why_are_we_meeting: Twenty-two people gather weekly so each team lead can report status to the group. The supplied purpose is information delivery, not interaction — but the meeting may also enable cross-team awareness, surface blockers, and allow anyone to ask questions across teams in real time.
what_must_be_true_when_we_leave: Each team lead has heard what every other team is working on
Any cross-team blockers or dependencies have surfaced and been flagged
Anyone with a question for another team has had a chance to ask it
who_needs_to_participate: Each team lead who holds status others need to hear
Anyone with authority to unblock cross-team issues when they surface
Anyone whose work depends on another team's status
before_the_meeting: Each team lead writes a three-to-five line status note and posts it before the meeting — attendees read, not listen, to routine updates
Anyone with a cross-team question or dependency flags it on the shared update so live time targets only those items

live_agenda.item: Flagged cross-team blockers and dependencies — only items teams identified in advance
live_agenda.why_live: These require real-time negotiation or escalation that a written update cannot resolve

live_agenda.item: Open floor: questions raised by the written updates that nobody flagged in advance
live_agenda.why_live: Unexpected questions benefit from immediate back-and-forth rather than async thread chains

live_agenda.item: Any time-sensitive coordination or announcements that require a live reaction
live_agenda.why_live: Some decisions need immediate acknowledgment or a quick group read to proceed

output.end_with: Close by naming any blocker that was raised and who owns it, then confirm whether next week's meeting is needed at full length or can be async if no flags are posted by a set cutoff.

cases.name: message-after-make-it-async
cases.guards: The follow-up a MAKE IT ASYNC verdict earns. The message must PROPOSE, never announce, and must never state that the visitor will skip.

input.meetingText: Weekly engineering all-hands. Standing 60-minute meeting, 22 attendees. Agenda: status updates from each team lead. No prep, no decisions, everyone reports out what they did last week. Recurring for six months.
input.better: Written updates from each lead before a deadline, plus a 20-minute sync kept only for what needs live discussion.

output.message: I wanted to raise something about the weekly all-hands — I think we could get the same value with less time cost for everyone. What if each lead submitted a short written update by Monday morning, and we kept a 20-minute sync for anything that actually needs live discussion? Happy to draft a template for the written updates if that would help get it off the ground.
output.why_it_lands: It offers a concrete structure rather than just a complaint, and the offer to do the legwork makes it easy for your manager to say yes.
output.if_they_say_no: Good to know — can you help me understand what the 60-minute format gives us that the shorter version would miss? That would help me get more out of it.
output.do_not_send: Any version that opens with 'this meeting is a waste of time' or implies the current format is your manager's failure — it puts them on the defensive before they can hear the idea.
